category.name: Mobile & lost devices
category.description: Lost, stolen, seized, or compromised laptops, phones, tablets, and removable media, plus MDM, SIM swap, and mobile malware incidents.

playbooks.name: Lost corporate laptop with full-disk encryption
playbooks.summary: Use when an employee reports a corporate laptop lost or misplaced and it is believed to be encrypted, to confirm encryption, cut access, and decide on notification.

preparation: Escrow BitLocker and FileVault recovery keys in Intune, Jamf, or AD for every laptop
Report encryption compliance per device in the MDM or endpoint management console
Publish a lost-device hotline and form that collects time, place, and device tag
Enable remote lock and wipe capability for all corporate laptops
identification: Confirm the asset tag and serial number in the CMDB and match it to the user
Verify encryption status and last compliance check-in for the device in the MDM console
Check whether the device was powered off, asleep, or locked when lost
Record the last check-in time, IP, and location reported by the endpoint agent
containment: Issue a remote lock or wipe command queued for the next check-in
Revoke the device's certificates and remove it from conditional access trusted devices
Reset the user's password and revoke refresh tokens in the identity provider
eradication: Mark the device as lost in the CMDB and the EDR console
Remove saved VPN profiles and Wi-Fi certificates tied to the device
Rotate the BitLocker or FileVault recovery key record so the escrowed key is retired
recovery: Issue a replacement laptop and restore user data from cloud sync or backup
Watch for the lost device checking in and confirm the wipe executed
File a police report if theft is suspected and record the report number
lessons: Record whether encryption evidence was strong enough to avoid breach notification
Track how quickly the loss was reported after it happened
Review the fleet for laptops reporting encryption non-compliance

splunk.title: Last sign-ins from the lost device
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin deviceDetail.deviceId="<device_id>" | stats latest(_time) as last values(ipAddress) as ips values(appDisplayName) as apps by userPrincipalName | convert ctime(last)

splunk.title: Any authentication from the device after reported loss
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.src="<device_hostname>" earliest=<loss_time> by Authentication.user Authentication.app Authentication.action _time span=1h

playbooks.name: Lost laptop without disk encryption
playbooks.summary: Use when a lost or stolen laptop was not encrypted, so data on disk must be presumed exposed and the team must scope data, credentials, and notification duties.

preparation: Alert on laptops that fail the encryption compliance policy for more than 7 days
Keep a data classification map of which roles store regulated data locally
Have privacy and legal contacts ready for breach notification decisions
Back up laptop user folders to cloud storage so their contents can be inventoried
identification: Confirm in the MDM console that the drive really was unencrypted
Inventory files synced from the laptop using the cloud backup or OneDrive file list
Identify regulated data such as PII, PHI, or cardholder data in that file list
List saved credentials, browser sessions, SSH keys, and VPN configs on the laptop
Interview the user about local-only files that were never synced
containment: Queue a remote wipe and lock in the MDM console
Revoke all sessions and tokens for the user across SaaS apps
Rotate SSH keys, API tokens, and service passwords that were stored on the laptop
Disable the device's VPN certificate
eradication: Remove trusted-device status from MFA and conditional access
Rotate any shared or team credentials found in local files
Invalidate browser-saved passwords by forcing resets for every site in the user's password manager export
recovery: Provide an encrypted replacement laptop and confirm encryption before handover
Monitor for use of the rotated credentials or the old device identity
Restore the user's files to the new laptop from cloud backup, not from removable copies
lessons: Determine with legal whether regulatory or customer notification is required
Find out why the encryption policy failed or was exempted for this laptop
Block network access for unencrypted endpoints via conditional access
Count remaining unencrypted laptops in the fleet and set a deadline

splunk.title: Files accessed by the user from the laptop in the last 30 days
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Workload IN ("OneDrive", "SharePoint") UserId=<suspect_user> Operation IN ("FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloadedFull") earliest=-30d | stats count by SourceFileName SiteUrl ClientIP

splunk.title: Use of credentials stored on the lost laptop
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.user=<suspect_user> earliest=<loss_time> by Authentication.src Authentication.app Authentication.action

splunk.title: Endpoints out of encryption compliance
splunk.spl: index=mdm sourcetype=intune:devices encryptionState!="encrypted" operatingSystem IN ("Windows", "macOS") | stats count by deviceName userPrincipalName complianceState

playbooks.name: Stolen phone with corporate email and apps
playbooks.summary: Use when an employee's phone holding corporate mail, chat, or MFA apps is stolen, to cut mailbox and app access and stop the phone being used as an MFA factor.

preparation: Require app protection policies that wipe corporate app data on remote command
Enforce a device passcode and auto-lock via MDM for any phone with corporate mail
Document how users report stolen phones outside business hours
Allow users to register a backup MFA method before they need it
identification: Identify the phone in the MDM or Exchange mobile device list for the user
Check the last sync time of Exchange ActiveSync or Outlook mobile for the device
Determine which MFA methods were bound to the phone, including authenticator push and SMS
Ask whether the phone was locked with a passcode or biometrics when stolen
containment: Send a selective wipe of corporate data through the MDM or app protection policy
Remove the phone from the user's registered MFA methods
Revoke all refresh tokens and sign the user out of every session
Block the device ID in Exchange ActiveSync
eradication: Re-register MFA on a new device after verifying the user's identity
Check the mailbox for new inbox rules or forwarding created after the theft
Remove the stolen phone from Teams, Slack, and other chat apps' active device lists
recovery: Enroll the replacement phone and confirm compliance before restoring mail
Help the user contact their carrier to suspend the line and blacklist the IMEI
Re-add the user to MFA with a hardware key or second authenticator as a backup factor
lessons: Measure time from theft to selective wipe
Review whether app protection policies covered every corporate app on the phone
Encourage phishing-resistant MFA that does not depend on a single phone

splunk.title: Mailbox activity from the stolen device
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Workload=Exchange UserId=<suspect_user> ClientInfoString IN ("*ActiveSync*", "*Outlook-iOS*", "*Outlook-Android*") | stats latest(_time) as last values(Operation) as ops by ClientIP ClientInfoString | convert ctime(last)

splunk.title: Inbox rules created after the theft
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity Operation IN ("New-InboxRule", "Set-InboxRule", "Set-Mailbox") UserId=<suspect_user> earliest=<theft_time> | table _time Operation Parameters{}.Name Parameters{}.Value ClientIP

playbooks.name: Malicious app on a BYOD phone with corporate access
playbooks.summary: Use when mobile threat defense or a user report shows a malicious or risky app on a personally owned phone that has corporate mail, chat, or file access.

preparation: Deploy mobile threat defense integrated with MDM and conditional access for BYOD
Use app protection policies so corporate data stays in managed apps only
Write a BYOD privacy statement covering what security can see on personal phones
Define which app risk levels block corporate access automatically
identification: Pull the MTD alert detail: app name, package ID, permissions, and risk reason
Check whether the app has accessibility, notification, or device admin permissions
Determine which corporate apps the user has on the device and data they hold
Search for the same package ID on other enrolled devices
containment: Let conditional access mark the device non-compliant and block corporate apps
Selectively wipe corporate data from managed apps on the device
Ask the user to uninstall the app and walk them through it
eradication: Confirm through MTD that the app is gone before restoring access
Reset the user's password if the app could read notifications or OTP codes
Add the package ID to the MTD and MDM blocked app list
recovery: Restore corporate access once the device reports compliant
Review the user's sign-ins for the week after the app was installed
Confirm managed app data was not copied to the malicious app via app protection logs
lessons: Measure how many BYOD devices had the same app installed
Check whether app protection prevented copy-out of corporate data
Share user guidance on sideloaded and lookalike apps

splunk.title: MTD detections for the package across devices
splunk.spl: index=mdm sourcetype=mtd:alerts app_package="<package_id>" | stats latest(_time) as last values(threat_type) as threat by device_id user os_version | convert ctime(last)

splunk.title: Sign-ins by the user from the mobile device
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin userPrincipalName=<suspect_user> deviceDetail.operatingSystem IN ("Android", "iOS") | stats count by appDisplayName ipAddress status.errorCode deviceDetail.isCompliant

playbooks.name: Suspected mercenary spyware on an executive's phone
playbooks.summary: Use when an executive receives a threat notification from Apple or Google, or shows signs of commercial spyware such as Pegasus-class implants on their phone.

preparation: Pre-arrange a specialist mobile forensics provider for high-risk staff
Offer Lockdown Mode and Advanced Protection guidance to executives who travel
Keep spare clean phones preconfigured for VIP replacement
Agree how executive privacy is protected during device forensics
identification: Preserve any Apple or Google threat notification email or in-app banner
Take an encrypted iTunes or ADB backup and sysdiagnose without resetting the phone
Run the backup through an open-source indicator checker such as MVT with current IOCs
Review which sensitive meetings, deals, or travel happened while the phone may be infected
Check whether other executives or assistants received similar notifications
containment: Move the executive to a clean replacement phone with a new number if possible
Keep the suspect phone powered on in airplane mode or a Faraday bag for analysis
Treat calls, messages, and microphone audio from the phone as possibly intercepted
eradication: Revoke all corporate tokens and app registrations tied to the suspect phone
Reset passwords for accounts used on the phone from a separate clean device
Retire or factory reset the original phone only after the forensic provider is done
recovery: Enable Lockdown Mode or equivalent on the replacement device
Brief the executive on rebooting daily and avoiding unknown links
Inform legal and communications if business-sensitive information may be exposed
lessons: Decide whether a formal threat assessment or law enforcement report is needed
Extend the VIP device protection program to assistants and family where appropriate
Review how fast the forensic provider engaged

splunk.title: Executive sign-ins from new locations or devices
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin userPrincipalName IN (<exec_users>) | stats count values(ipAddress) as ips values(location.countryOrRegion) as countries by deviceDetail.displayName deviceDetail.operatingSystem

splunk.title: DNS lookups from the executive phone's corporate Wi-Fi IP
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=stream:dns src_ip=<phone_wifi_ip> | stats count by query | sort count | head 200

playbooks.name: SIM swap against an employee's phone number
playbooks.summary: Use when an employee's phone suddenly loses service or the carrier reports a SIM or eSIM change, and SMS-based MFA or recovery for corporate accounts may be hijacked.

preparation: Remove SMS and voice as allowed MFA methods for privileged and finance users
Ask staff to add a carrier account PIN or port-out lock to their numbers
Keep corporate carrier account contacts for fast SIM reversal on company lines
Monitor for MFA phone number changes in the identity provider
identification: Confirm with the employee from another channel that their phone shows no service
Check the identity provider for SMS MFA challenges and password resets after the outage
Review sign-ins for the user from new devices or IPs since the SIM change
Check if personal accounts with the same phone number reported resets too
containment: Remove the phone number from the user's MFA and self-service password reset methods
Reset the user's password and revoke all active sessions
Contact the carrier, or help the employee contact theirs, to reverse the SIM swap
Disable payment or approval workflows the user owns until verified
eradication: Remove MFA methods or devices the attacker enrolled after the swap
Delete mailbox forwarding or rules created by the attacker
Register a phishing-resistant authenticator such as a FIDO2 key
recovery: Restore the user's access after in-person or video identity verification
Monitor the account for new MFA registrations over the next 30 days
Confirm with the carrier that the number is back on the employee's SIM with a port-out lock
lessons: Count users still using SMS MFA and set a migration target
Add a detection for SMS-based reset followed by MFA method change
Review whether help desk verification could have been bypassed the same way

splunk.title: SMS MFA and reset events for the user
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=okta:im2 actor.alternateId=<suspect_user> eventType IN ("user.mfa.factor.activate", "user.account.reset_password", "system.sms.send_factor_verify_message", "user.mfa.factor.update") | table _time eventType client.ipAddress client.userAgent.rawUserAgent outcome.result

splunk.title: New MFA factors registered after the SIM change
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:audit activityDisplayName IN ("User registered security info", "User changed default security info") targetResources{}.userPrincipalName=<suspect_user> earliest=<swap_time> | table _time activityDisplayName initiatedBy.user.ipAddress

playbooks.name: Jailbroken or rooted device accessing corporate data
playbooks.summary: Use when MDM or MTD reports a jailbroken iPhone or rooted Android device that still has corporate mail, files, or app sessions.

preparation: Configure compliance policy to flag jailbreak and root detection signals
Block non-compliant devices from corporate apps through conditional access
State the jailbreak and root rule in the acceptable use and BYOD policies
identification: Confirm the jailbreak or root flag in MDM and MTD and rule out a false positive
Check which corporate apps and accounts were active on the device
Look for sideloaded apps or tweak frameworks that can read other apps' data
Determine how long the device was rooted before detection
containment: Block the device from corporate resources via compliance and conditional access
Selectively wipe corporate containers and managed apps
Revoke tokens issued to the device
eradication: Require the user to restore stock firmware before re-enrollment
Reset the user's password if credentials were stored on the device
Remove the device's certificates for Wi-Fi and VPN
recovery: Re-enroll the device only after attestation passes again
Monitor the user's sign-ins for unknown devices for two weeks
Reissue Wi-Fi and VPN certificates to the re-enrolled device only after compliance passes
lessons: Measure lag between jailbreak and MDM detection
Evaluate hardware-backed attestation such as Play Integrity or App Attest for corporate apps
Remind staff of the consequences of rooting corporate-enabled phones

splunk.title: Devices flagged jailbroken or rooted
splunk.spl: index=mdm sourcetype=intune:devices (jailBroken="True" OR complianceState="noncompliant") | stats latest(_time) as last by deviceName userPrincipalName operatingSystem osVersion jailBroken | convert ctime(last)

splunk.title: Corporate app access from the flagged device
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin deviceDetail.deviceId="<device_id>" | stats count by appDisplayName conditionalAccessStatus status.errorCode

playbooks.name: MDM console compromised or mass device wipe issued
playbooks.summary: Use when someone abuses the MDM or UEM console (Intune, Jamf, Workspace ONE) to wipe, lock, or push scripts to many devices, or an MDM admin account is compromised.

preparation: Require multi-admin approval for wipe, retire, and script deployment in the MDM
Limit MDM global admins to a small group using phishing-resistant MFA
Back up MDM configuration profiles, scripts, and app assignments
Keep a list of business-critical devices that would need priority rebuild
identification: Pull MDM audit logs for wipe, retire, lock, and script deployment actions
Identify the admin account, source IP, and session used for the actions
Count devices affected and categorize them by business function
Check for new MDM admin roles, API apps, or certificates created recently
containment: Disable the compromised admin account and revoke its sessions
Cancel pending wipe or script actions not yet delivered to devices
Remove rogue API apps, service principals, or enrollment tokens
Freeze MDM admin changes to a named break-glass account only
eradication: Delete malicious scripts, profiles, and app assignments the attacker deployed
Rotate APNs certificates, enrollment tokens, and MDM connectors if exposed
Investigate how the admin credentials were obtained and close that path
recovery: Rebuild wiped devices starting with priority roles using Autopilot or Automated Device Enrollment
Restore configuration from the MDM backup and verify policy assignments
Communicate to staff how to re-enroll and restore data from cloud backups
lessons: Measure how many devices were wiped before the action was stopped
Turn on multi-admin approval if it was not enforced
Add an alert for bulk device actions above a threshold

splunk.title: Bulk wipe and retire actions in Intune audit logs
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:intune:audit activityType IN ("wipe ManagedDevice", "retire ManagedDevice", "remoteLock ManagedDevice") | bin _time span=10m | stats dc(resources{}.resourceId) as devices values(actor.userPrincipalName) as admins by _time | where devices > 5

splunk.title: MDM admin sign-ins by source
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin appDisplayName IN ("Microsoft Intune", "Microsoft Intune portal extension") userPrincipalName IN (<mdm_admins>) | stats count values(ipAddress) as ips by userPrincipalName status.errorCode

splunk.title: Script and app deployments created by the admin
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:intune:audit actor.userPrincipalName=<suspect_admin> activityType IN ("*DeviceManagementScript*", "*MobileApp*", "*DeviceConfiguration*") | table _time activityType resources{}.displayName

playbooks.name: Rogue MDM or configuration profile installed on a device
playbooks.summary: Use when a phone or Mac has an unknown configuration profile, root certificate, VPN, or MDM enrollment that could intercept traffic or control the device.

preparation: Report installed profiles and trusted root certificates from MDM-managed devices
Block manual profile installation on supervised iOS devices
Teach users that profile install prompts from websites or texts are suspicious
identification: List all configuration profiles on the device and their signing identity
Check for unknown trusted root CAs, global HTTP proxies, or VPN payloads
Ask the user how the profile was installed: link, email, QR code, or Wi-Fi portal
Search MDM inventory for the same profile identifier on other devices
containment: Remove the rogue profile or have the user delete it in device settings
Block the profile's proxy or VPN server address at the corporate egress
Treat traffic since installation as intercepted and revoke the user's sessions
eradication: Reset passwords for accounts the user signed into while the profile was active
Block the distribution URL or domain on secure web gateway and DNS
Revoke and reissue any corporate certificates installed on the device while the rogue root was trusted
recovery: Confirm the device shows only the corporate MDM profile after cleanup
Monitor for reinstallation of the same profile identifier
Restore the user's corporate app access only after a fresh compliance check
lessons: Supervise corporate iOS devices so profile installs can be restricted
Add MDM reporting for non-corporate root certificates
Use this example in phishing awareness material

splunk.title: Devices reporting the unknown profile identifier
splunk.spl: index=mdm sourcetype=jamf:inventory profile_identifier="<profile_id>" | stats latest(_time) as last by device_name username serial_number | convert ctime(last)

splunk.title: Proxy or VPN traffic to the rogue endpoint
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip=<ioc_ip> by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.action

playbooks.name: Lost USB drive containing sensitive data
playbooks.summary: Use when a USB stick or external drive holding customer, employee, or confidential data is lost, to establish what was on it, whether it was encrypted, and notification needs.

preparation: Enforce BitLocker To Go or hardware-encrypted USB drives through device control
Log file copies to removable media in the DLP or EDR platform
Keep a register of approved encrypted USB drives by serial and owner
identification: Get the drive's make, serial, and whether it was an approved encrypted model
Pull DLP or EDR file-copy logs for the drive serial to list what was written to it
Classify the copied files for PII, PHI, financial, or confidential content
Estimate the number of individuals whose data was on the drive
containment: Search the last known locations and lost-and-found with facilities
Rotate any passwords, keys, or secrets that were stored on the drive
Revoke the drive from the approved device register
eradication: Delete remaining copies of the data from other unmanaged media the user holds
Block the drive serial in device control in case it resurfaces
Remove the data set from the user's local folders if it no longer needs to be held
recovery: Give the user an approved encrypted drive or a secure file sharing alternative
Prepare notification letters with legal if unencrypted personal data was on the drive
Set up a monitored mailbox or call line for individuals receiving notification letters
lessons: Decide whether unencrypted USB write access should be blocked company-wide
Review why the user needed to carry data on removable media
Track how complete the DLP file-copy evidence was

splunk.title: Files written to the lost USB drive
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=dlp:endpoint action="copy_to_removable" device_serial="<usb_serial>" | stats count values(file_name) as files values(classification) as classes by user host

splunk.title: Removable media writes by the user in the last 90 days
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational EventCode=11 User="*<suspect_user>" TargetFilename IN ("E:\\*", "F:\\*", "G:\\*") earliest=-90d | stats count by host TargetFilename

playbooks.name: Stolen tablet from a field worker
playbooks.summary: Use when a ruggedized or shared tablet used by field technicians, drivers, or inspectors is stolen, including from a vehicle, along with any work orders or customer data on it.

preparation: Run field tablets in MDM kiosk or dedicated-device mode with a locked app set
Enable location reporting on field tablets where policy and law allow
Use per-device service accounts so a stolen tablet can be cut off alone
Keep cached offline work order data minimal and encrypted
identification: Confirm the tablet's device ID, assigned crew, and vehicle from the fleet register
Pull the last location and check-in time from the MDM console
List customer addresses, work orders, or site access codes cached on the tablet
Check whether the field app session or device certificate was used after the theft
containment: Send a full wipe to the tablet through the MDM console
Disable the tablet's service account and revoke its device certificate
Change site gate or lockbox codes that were stored on the tablet
eradication: Remove the device from the field service platform's trusted device list
Invalidate any offline tokens the field app issued to the tablet
Reset the field app PIN or shared crew login that was used on the tablet
recovery: Provision a replacement tablet from the spare pool and enroll it in kiosk mode
File a police report with the device serial and IMEI
Notify affected customers if their personal data or access codes were on the device
lessons: Review vehicle storage rules for devices left unattended
Track replacement time to keep field crews productive
Reduce the amount of customer data the field app caches offline

splunk.title: Field app API calls from the stolen tablet
splunk.spl: index=app sourcetype=fieldservice:api device_id="<device_id>" earliest=<theft_time> | stats count values(endpoint) as endpoints by src_ip user

splunk.title: MDM check-ins and location for the tablet
splunk.spl: index=mdm sourcetype=intune:devices deviceId="<device_id>" | table _time deviceName lastSyncDateTime managementState complianceState

playbooks.name: Device left at border or seized by customs
playbooks.summary: Use when a traveling employee's laptop or phone is inspected, imaged, retained, or confiscated by border or customs officials, or left behind at a checkpoint.

preparation: Issue loaner travel laptops and phones with minimal data for high-risk destinations
Brief travelers on what to do and whom to call if a device is inspected
Have legal counsel guidance on privileged data and device searches by country
identification: Record which device, where, when, and whether it was out of the traveler's sight
Ask whether the traveler unlocked the device or gave passwords to officials
List the data, accounts, and privileged legal material on the device
Check whether the device was returned and whether it was powered off throughout
containment: Revoke the device's tokens, certificates, and MFA registrations
Reset passwords for every account accessible from the device
Treat a returned device as untrusted and do not reconnect it to the corporate network
eradication: Send the returned device for forensic review or reimage it before reuse
Replace hardware security keys that were in custody with the device
Rotate VPN, SSH, and API credentials that were stored on the seized device
recovery: Provide a clean replacement device to the traveler at the destination
Review sign-in logs for the traveler's accounts for unknown access
Debrief the traveler and record officials' agency and reference numbers for legal
lessons: Involve legal on whether privileged or customer data was disclosed
Update the travel security program for destinations with device searches
Track whether loaner devices were used as recommended

splunk.title: Sign-ins from the seized device after seizure
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=azure:aad:signin deviceDetail.deviceId="<device_id>" earliest=<seizure_time> | table _time userPrincipalName appDisplayName ipAddress location.countryOrRegion status.errorCode

splunk.title: Traveler account access by country
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.user=<suspect_user> earliest=-14d by Authentication.src Authentication.app Authentication.action | iplocation Authentication.src | stats sum(count) by Country Authentication.app

playbooks.name: Smishing text led to a malicious APK install
playbooks.summary: Use when an employee clicked a text message link and sideloaded an Android APK, such as a fake delivery or bank app, on a phone with corporate access.

preparation: Disallow installs from unknown sources on corporate-managed Android work profiles
Give staff a simple way to forward suspicious texts to the SOC
Keep MTD with sideloaded app detection on devices with corporate access
identification: Collect the SMS text, sender number, and link from the user's screenshot
Identify the installed APK package name and its requested permissions
Check whether the app was granted accessibility or SMS read permissions
Search proxy and DNS logs for the smishing domain from other corporate devices
Find other employees who received the same text
containment: Block the device from corporate access until the APK is removed
Block the smishing and C2 domains on DNS and secure web gateway
Reset passwords and revoke sessions for accounts used on the phone
eradication: Have the user boot into safe mode and uninstall the APK, or factory reset
Remove the APK's device admin rights before uninstalling if it holds them
Report the smishing domain to the registrar and the carrier spam service
recovery: Restore access after MTD reports the device clean
Advise the user to check personal banking apps for fraud
Watch the user's accounts for OTP-intercept style sign-ins over the next two weeks
lessons: Add the lure theme to smishing awareness content
Track how many recipients reported versus clicked
Review whether the work profile restrictions applied to this device

splunk.title: Corporate devices resolving the smishing domain
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=stream:dns query IN ("*<smish_domain>") | stats count min(_time) as first by src_ip query | convert ctime(first)

splunk.title: APK downloads seen at the web proxy
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*.apk" by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.http_user_agent

playbooks.name: Employee reports their corporate phone is hacked
playbooks.summary: Use when a user reports battery drain, strange pop-ups, messages they did not send, or account alerts and believes their corporate phone is compromised, before any evidence is confirmed.

preparation: Publish a mobile triage questionnaire for the service desk
Ensure MDM collects installed app inventory for corporate phones
Keep a loaner phone pool so a suspect phone can be swapped quickly
identification: Interview the user on symptoms, when they began, and recent installs or links
Pull the phone's installed app list and profiles from the MDM console
Check MTD for network, app, or OS risk detections on the phone
Review sign-ins and MFA prompts the user did not initiate
Check the OS version against current security patches
containment: Swap the phone for a loaner if any credible indicator is found
Revoke sessions and require a password change if unexpected sign-ins exist
Ask the user to stop using the phone for corporate MFA until triage is complete
eradication: Remove any unapproved apps or profiles identified in the inventory
Update the phone to the latest OS and security patch level
Factory reset and re-enroll the phone if indicators remain unexplained
recovery: Return the phone after reset and confirm compliance in MDM
Follow up with the user after a week to confirm symptoms are gone
Remove the loaner phone from the user once their own device is returned clean
lessons: Record whether symptoms were benign such as adware, a full disk, or OS bugs
Refine the service desk questionnaire using this case
Track how many hacked-phone reports turn out to be real compromises

splunk.title: MFA push prompts the user did not initiate
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=okta:im2 actor.alternateId=<suspect_user> eventType="system.push.send_factor_verify_push" earliest=-7d | stats count by client.ipAddress outcome.result

splunk.title: Installed apps reported by MDM for the phone
splunk.spl: index=mdm sourcetype=intune:detectedapps deviceId="<device_id>" | stats latest(version) as version by displayName publisher | sort displayName

playbooks.name: Departed employee has not returned company devices
playbooks.summary: Use when a former employee or contractor keeps a company laptop, phone, or token after their last day and the device may still hold data or working access.

preparation: Tie HR termination events to automatic account disable and device lock
Track device assignment per person in the asset system for offboarding checks
Prepare prepaid return shipping kits for remote employees
identification: List every device assigned to the person from the asset system and MDM
Check last check-in time and network location for each device
Confirm that the person's accounts were disabled on schedule
Review DLP and cloud logs for large downloads in the last 30 days of employment
containment: Issue remote lock and wipe for each unreturned device
Revoke device certificates, VPN profiles, and hardware token assignments
Disable any personal device enrollments still syncing corporate data
eradication: Remove the person from shared drives, groups, and SaaS apps that bypass SSO
Rotate shared credentials the person knew
Reassign or close any mailboxes and OneDrive storage the person still owns
recovery: Send formal return requests through HR and then legal if ignored
Mark the device as lost if not returned by the deadline and record write-off
Inspect and reimage any device that is returned before reissuing it
lessons: Measure how many departures leave devices outstanding past 14 days
Fix gaps between HR systems and identity or MDM deprovisioning
Decide whether final pay or contract terms should address device return

splunk.title: Activity by the departed user after termination
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.user=<suspect_user> earliest=<term_date> by Authentication.app Authentication.src Authentication.action

splunk.title: Bulk downloads in the final 30 days of employment
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=o365:management:activity UserId=<suspect_user> Operation IN ("FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloadedFull") earliest=-30d@d | bin _time span=1d | stats count by _time | where count > 100

splunk.title: MDM check-ins from unreturned devices
splunk.spl: index=mdm sourcetype=intune:devices userPrincipalName=<suspect_user> | stats latest(lastSyncDateTime) as last_sync by deviceName serialNumber managementState
